title: Passing Edom, Moab, and Ammon; Defeating Sihon
summary: Moses recalls the long years around Mount Seir and God's command to turn north. Israel must not provoke Edom, Moab, or Ammon, because God has given those peoples their lands as he is giving Israel its own. After thirty-eight years, when the generation of fighting men has died, Israel crosses the Zered and the Arnon. Sihon, king of Heshbon, refuses a peaceful passage, and God delivers him and his land to Israel.
story: Chapter 1 ended with Israel defeated at Hormah and staying at Kadesh a very long time. This chapter covers the long wandering in a few verses and then slows down as the new generation begins to move toward the land. It marks a turning point in two ways. First, verses 14-16 record that the whole generation of fighting men who left Egypt has now died, as God swore; the sentence of Kadesh is complete. Second, after decades of defeat and delay, Israel wins the first victory Moses recounts in this retelling, against Sihon (Numbers 21:1-3 records an earlier victory over the king of Arad). The chapter carries the story from failure to renewed obedience, and chapter 3 continues with the defeat of Og and the division of the land east of the Jordan.
historical:
Israel's route runs through the kingdoms east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. Edom (the descendants of Esau) lay south of the Dead Sea in the region of Mount Seir; Moab lay east of the Dead Sea between the Zered and the Arnon valleys; Ammon lay further north and east, around the headwaters of the Jabbok. The Brook of Zered, usually identified with the Wadi el-Hasa, marked the border between Edom and Moab, and the Arnon (Wadi Mujib) the northern border of Moab. Elath and Ezion-geber (verse 8) lay at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba. Sihon's kingdom, centered on Heshbon, occupied land north of the Arnon that had earlier belonged to Moab (Numbers 21:26). Numbers 21:21-32 gives a parallel account of the battle at Jahaz.

Archaeologists have debated how developed the kingdoms of Edom, Moab, and Ammon were in the late Bronze Age, since much of the evidence for organized states in the region comes from later centuries. Some scholars take this as evidence that the account reflects a later period; others argue that the peoples named could have existed as tribal or smaller political groups before fuller statehood.
cultural:
The parenthetical notes in verses 10-12 and 20-23 give old traditions about the peoples who lived in these lands before Edom, Moab, and Ammon. The Emim, Zamzummim, and Anakim were remembered as tall and numerous peoples and were all counted among the Rephaim. The word rephaim appears elsewhere in the Old Testament for the shades of the dead (Isaiah 14:9), and in texts from ancient Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, the rephaim are associated with the dead or with ancestral heroes. How these uses relate to the peoples in Deuteronomy is debated. The Horites lived in Seir before Edom; the Avvim were displaced by the Caphtorites, a people from Caphtor, usually identified with Crete, whom Amos names as the origin of the Philistines (Amos 9:7).

In the ancient Near East, a people moving through foreign territory would ask permission and pay for food and water, as Israel does here. Refusing passage was a hostile act, and the offer of peace before battle anticipates the law of Deuteronomy 20:10, which requires Israel to offer terms of peace to a city before attacking it.
literary: The chapter is structured by God's commands and Israel's movements, with the recurring pattern of God speaking, Israel obeying, and Moses reporting. Three encounters are told in parallel: Edom (verses 1-8), Moab (verses 9-15), and Ammon (verses 16-23). In each case God forbids Israel to provoke the people, because he has given them their land. Each is followed by a note on the peoples who lived there before, showing that God has already been at work among other nations. The fourth encounter, Sihon, breaks the pattern: God gives this land to Israel. The parenthetical notes read like an ancient historian's aside, interrupting the speech to explain a name or a place. The phrase “to this day” (verse 22) suggests that some of these notes were added from a later perspective.

outline.t: Passing by Edom without provoking them
Moab is not to be attacked; the former inhabitants
Crossing the Zered: the old generation has died
Ammon is not to be attacked; the former inhabitants
God gives Sihon into Israel's hand
An offer of peace and Sihon's refusal
The defeat of Sihon at Jahaz

doctrines.note: God assigns lands not only to Israel but also to Edom, Moab, and Ammon, and he has displaced peoples before. He rules the history of all nations, not only his own people.
“The LORD your God has been with you these forty years, and you have lacked nothing.” Even in the years of judgment, God provided for the generation that would inherit.
The death of the whole generation of fighting men before Israel crossed the Zered shows God's oath being carried out. His warnings and his promises both come true.

words.note: Charam, to devote to destruction. Something under the ban (cherem) was set apart for God and could not be used for ordinary purposes, which in war meant the destruction of people and sometimes property. Its use here and in the conquest is one of the hardest parts of the Old Testament; see the hard question below.

Qashah, to be hard or make hard. God made Sihon's spirit stubborn, as he hardened Pharaoh in Exodus. The verb describes a heart set against God's purposes. The Bible holds together God's sovereign hand and the human responsibility of the one who refuses.

Garah, to provoke or stir up conflict. Israel is repeatedly told not to provoke Edom, Moab, or Ammon. The restraint is striking: Israel may not seize land God has not given, and God protects the inheritance of these other peoples as he protects Israel's.

Yerushah, possession. It describes land held as a possession by inheritance. God has given Seir to Esau and Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession, using the same language he uses for Israel's land.

christ: The chapter shows a God who rules all nations, which the New Testament confirms. Paul told the Athenians that God “determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands” (Acts 17:26), echoing the conviction that God assigns the nations their places, as he does for Edom, Moab, and Ammon here. The long delay until an unbelieving generation had died also shapes the New Testament's warnings: Hebrews uses the wilderness years to urge believers to hold fast in faith. The chapter's hardest element, the destruction of Sihon's people, belongs to a particular moment in Israel's history; the New Testament does not repeat it but reinterprets the warfare of God's people as a spiritual struggle (Ephesians 6:12), with Christ himself bearing the judgment for sin. The link here is one of theme and contrast rather than prediction.

hard.q: How should we understand the destruction of Sihon's cities, including women and children, and God hardening Sihon's heart?
hard.a: Verse 34 says Israel devoted the people of every city to destruction, “including women and children.” This is deeply troubling, and Christians have answered in several ways. Some stress that God as judge of all the earth has the right to judge nations for their sin, as Genesis 15:16 speaks of the sin of the Amorites reaching its full measure, and that Sihon was offered peace and chose war. Others point out that ancient Near Eastern war reports, such as the Moabite Stone, used sweeping language of total destruction, and suggest that such language may be hyperbolic, since the same peoples reappear later. Others emphasize that these commands were limited to a unique moment and a specific land and are never given as a pattern for later warfare. On the hardening of Sihon's heart, many interpreters note that God gives people over to what they have already chosen, as with Pharaoh, who also hardened his own heart; others emphasize God's sovereign purpose without denying Sihon's responsibility. Believers often confess that God is just while admitting that these passages remain hard. They should never be used to justify violence.

questions: God told Israel not to take the land he had given to Edom, Moab, and Ammon. What does this say about God's care for peoples outside Israel?
“You have lacked nothing” was said of forty years in the wilderness. Looking back on a hard season of your own, where can you see God's provision?
The first victory came only after the old generation had passed away. What might it mean to wait for God's timing when you are eager to move forward?
